front: What is the practical difference between List and Set when choosing a collection type?
back: A List preserves an order and allows duplicate elements accessed by index, while a Set enforces uniqueness and generally has no positional access.
accepted_answers: List allows duplicates and index access; Set enforces uniqueness
hint: Ask whether duplicates are meaningful and whether order or position matters.

front: Why can a Stream only be consumed once?
back: A stream models a pipeline of operations over a source, and once a terminal operation runs it closes that pipeline, so calling another terminal operation on the same stream throws IllegalStateException.
accepted_answers: streams are single-use pipelines closed after a terminal operation
hint: Create a new stream from the source if you need to traverse it again.

front: Why does generic type information not exist at runtime in Java?
back: Generics are implemented through type erasure, so the compiler checks type parameters at compile time and then replaces them with their bounds or Object in the bytecode, leaving no generic type info to inspect at runtime.
accepted_answers: generics use type erasure so parameter types are removed from the compiled bytecode
hint: This is why you cannot create a generic array or check instanceof List<String> directly.

front: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
back: Comparable defines a class's single natural ordering through compareTo, while Comparator defines an external, reusable ordering through compare that can be swapped without changing the class.
accepted_answers: Comparable is natural ordering on the class; Comparator is an external reusable ordering
hint: Only one Comparable ordering can exist per class, but many Comparators can.

front: Why is ConcurrentModificationException thrown when a collection is structurally modified outside its iterator during iteration?
back: Most collection iterators track a modification count on the source and fail fast by throwing ConcurrentModificationException as soon as they detect a structural change that did not go through the iterator itself.
accepted_answers: iterators fail fast when they detect a structural change made outside the iterator
hint: Use the iterator's own remove() instead of modifying the source collection directly.

front: A HashMap<String, Integer> is populated, then the key class's hashCode() implementation is changed and the application is redeployed without clearing the map. What happens to get() lookups for previously stored keys after the redeploy?
back: Lookups can fail to find previously stored entries because each entry's stored bucket was computed with the old hashCode implementation, so the new hashCode no longer matches the bucket the value actually lives in.
accepted_answers: lookups can fail because entries were bucketed using the old hashCode and never rehashed
hint: HashMap never rehashes existing entries just because the hashCode implementation changed in code.

front: A List<Integer> built from Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3) throws UnsupportedOperationException when .add() is called on it. Why?
back: Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by the original array, so structural changes like add or remove are not supported even though set() works.
accepted_answers: Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list view over an array, so add and remove are unsupported
hint: The list is a view over a fixed-size array, not a growable ArrayList.

front: Calling list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> sometimes removes a different element than the caller expected. What is the most likely mistake?
back: remove(int) removes by index while remove(Object) removes by value; passing an int literal like 1 calls the index overload, not the value overload, so it may not remove the intended element.
accepted_answers: remove(int) removes by index, not by value; an int literal picks the index overload
hint: Autoboxing the argument to Integer.valueOf(1) would select the Object overload instead.

front: A for-each loop over a List<String> throws ConcurrentModificationException when the loop body calls list.remove(item). How should this be fixed?
back: Use the iterator's own remove() method (or Collection.removeIf, or build a new filtered list) instead of modifying the source list directly during a for-each loop.
accepted_answers: use the iterator's remove(), removeIf, or build a new filtered list instead of mutating during for-each
hint: A for-each loop uses an iterator under the hood and does not expect direct list mutation.

front: A method returns List<String>, and storing the result as List<Object> is a compile error even though String is an Object. Why does the compiler reject this without a wildcard?
back: Generics are invariant, so List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>; allowing it would let incompatible elements be added through the List<Object> reference, breaking type safety.
accepted_answers: generics are invariant so List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>
hint: Use List<? extends Object> if you only need to read elements.

front: A parallel stream over a small list of 5 elements runs slower than the sequential version in production. What is the most likely explanation?
back: For small data sets the overhead of splitting work and coordinating threads outweighs the benefit of parallelism, so parallel streams are only worthwhile for large data sets or expensive per-element work.
accepted_answers: coordination overhead outweighs the benefit for small data sets or cheap per-element work
hint: Parallelism has fixed coordination costs regardless of how little work there is to do.
